title: Something New
full_review:
Contrary to its title's claim, there's not much fresh about "Something New" (Focus).
Interracial romances are, in fact, nothing new, at least not in Hollywood where they've been used as fodder by filmmakers from Stanley Kramer to Spike Lee.

Directed with admitted visual vibrancy by Sanaa Hamri, the otherwise lackluster love story centers on Kenya (Sanaa Lathan), a buttoned-down African-American executive at a prestigious Los Angeles accounting firm, where she is in line for a partnership. Ivy League educated, Kenya is beautiful and brainy, but alas, unable to find a man, at least not one who passes muster based on her lengthy checklist of desirable traits.

When not logging late office hours, she commiserates with her circle of single, professional girlfriends (Wendy Raquel Robinson, Golden Brooks and Taraji P. Henson) about the scarcity of what they consider ideal African-American mates.

A co-worker sets her up with a blind date, who, much to Kenya's surprise, turns out to be white. Though it doesn't bother him, Kenya is visibly uncomfortable and, making a lame excuse, bolts.
At the co-worker's engagement party, a compliment about the floral arrangements prompts the bride-to-be to introduce Kenya to her landscaper, who, as fate would have it, is the jilted blind date, Brian (Simon Baker).

Denying her obvious attraction, Kenya hires the free-spirited Brian to rehabilitate her disheveled backyard. As her garden starts to blossom, so inevitably does their romance, with predictable reactions from her Afro-centric coterie.

The supporting cast includes Alfre Woodard and Earl Billings as Kenya's socialite parents, and Donald Faison as her philandering younger brother. Blair Underwood plays a suave lawyer and Brian's main competition, who embodies everything Kenya thought she wanted in a man.
Like last year's "Guess Who?" "Something New" explores, in a less superficial manner, society's unspoken prejudices, both black and white, while similarly reversing racial stereotypes.

Lathan, who recently wowed Broadway audiences in "A Raisin in the Sun," sparkles, conveying vulnerability beneath the Type A facade. There is also credible chemistry between her and the equally appealing Baker. (What starts out as lust deepens into genuine affection.)

Unfortunately, the sentimental "love is colorblind" message is weedy with cliches and preachy dialogue, capped off by a preposterous climax at a cotillion. What this film really needed was a script doctor, not a lawn doctor.

The film contains several implied sexual encounters, a scene of passionate groping, a tacit approval of premarital sex and a suggestive dance performance, as well as some crude sexual language and humor and crass expressions. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
